text:
Evidence supports testing the objective before adding history fusion, but does not establish it as this benchmark’s main limitation. [gSASRec, IJCAI 2024](https://www.ijcai.org/proceedings/2024/939) attributes SASRec degradation to overconfidence from negative-sampled BCE; its practical alternative is gBCE with more negatives, recommending calibration t=0.75 and 128–256 negatives. These are starting points, not guaranteed optima. [Scalable Cross-Entropy, RecSys 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.18721) offers another architecture-preserving alternative: approximate full-catalog CE using informative high-scoring items, reporting competitive accuracy with substantially lower memory use.

Harder negatives require caution in sparse implicit feedback: an unobserved item may still be relevant. [R2NS, WWW 2026](https://renzhaochun.github.io/assets/pdf/WWW_2026_Camera_Ready.pdf) reports that deterministic hardest-negative sampling can underperform uniform sampling; its approach introduces warm-up, adaptive candidate selection and stochastic sampling to mitigate instability and false negatives. A [2024 sampling study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17276) also finds that sampling performance depends on dataset characteristics and popularity bias. Thus, large training margins against sampled negatives do not establish top-10 ranking quality against the evaluator’s candidates.

Practical inference: freeze SASRec architecture, histories, seeds and optimizer; first compare the existing uniform candidate-softmax objective against gBCE at the same negative count, then vary negative count separately. Add full CE where affordable or SCE as a subsequent comparison. Test a warm-started uniform/hard-negative mixture separately because it changes sampling as well as optimization; exclude known training positives without consulting held-out labels. Select using the pinned four-category macro validation HR@10 and report category results and GPU cost. Published gains do not establish gains under this specific 100-candidate protocol.
